cards.text: Friend, the prophet Hosea is in the middle of a hard message for Israel. He opens with a picture: “Israel was a luxuriant vine, yielding fruit for himself.” Israel is THRIVING.

cards.question: But watch what Israel does with all that fruit. The more the fruit increased, the more Israel increased the ___.
As Israel's land produced better, Israel tore down its sacred pillars.

cards.text: Then Hosea says it plain: their hearts are devious, and now they must bear their guilt. Not confused, not having an off week. DEVIOUS.

cards.question: Israel has been building up altars and sacred pillars. So what will the LORD do to them?

cards.text: Next, Hosea tells what the people will say about having a king. And friend, it is NOT a pep rally.

cards.question: The people will say, 'We have no king.' What reason do they give?

answers.text: We do not revere the LORD
The LORD has not sent one
We do not honor our elders

cards.question: Then the people say a king can do a lot for them.

cards.text: Their promises are mere words, and they make covenants with false oaths. It's like me telling a baker, 'I'll keep this story short,' and friend, I have NEVER kept a story short.

cards.question: All those broken promises grow into something. Judgment springs up like poisonous ___ in the furrows of a field.

cards.text: Now Hosea turns to the calf of Beth-aven, an idol in Israel, and says the people of Samaria, a city of Israel, will fear for it. Friend, when your god needs YOU to do the worrying, something has gone sideways.

cards.question: The calf's people and its idolatrous priests will mourn over the calf of Beth-aven. Why?

answers.text: It is taken from them into exile
It is melted down in a fire
It is smashed by a prophet

cards.question: The calf of Beth-aven gets carried off to ___ as tribute to the great king.

cards.text: Hosea uses Ephraim as another name for Israel, and here he says it both ways: Ephraim will be seized with shame, and Israel will be ashamed of its wooden idols.

cards.question: When Samaria is carried off, Hosea says her king will be left behind.

cards.text: Samaria goes with her king, carried off “like a twig on the surface of the water.” Just floating wherever the water says.
The high places of Aven will be destroyed, and Hosea calls it the sin of Israel. Thorns and thistles will overgrow their altars.

cards.question: Then the people of Israel call out to the mountains and the hills. What do they want?

cards.text: Then Hosea reaches WAY back, to the days of a town called Gibeah. He tells Israel they have sinned since the days of Gibeah.

cards.question: Hosea says Israel has moved far past the sins of Gibeah.

cards.text: Nope: “and there you have remained.” Friend, I spent YEARS stuck in a junk drawer, and even I think that's a long time to stay put.
Then the LORD says He will chasten them when He pleases. Not on Israel's schedule, friend. On HIS.

cards.question: ___ will be gathered against Israel to put them in bondage for their double transgression.

cards.text: New picture: Ephraim is a well-trained heifer that loves to thresh. She knows her job and she LOVES it, like me with a fresh batch of dough.

cards.question: But the LORD has other plans for that heifer. He says, 'I will place a ___ on her fair neck.'
The LORD says He will harness Ephraim. Then Judah, the southern kingdom, and Jacob, another name for Israel, get put to work. Doing what?

cards.text: And then comes an invitation: “Sow for yourselves righteousness and reap the fruit of loving devotion; break up your unplowed ground.” That's dough straight out of the fridge, friend: you can't roll out ANYTHING until you break it up first.

cards.question: Israel is told to break up the unplowed ground. Why now?

answers.text: It is time to seek the LORD
The ground will soon be sold

cards.question: If Israel seeks the LORD until He comes, He will send righteousness on them like ___.

cards.text: But here's what they actually did: they plowed wickedness, reaped injustice and ate the fruit of lies.

cards.question: Hosea says Israel trusted in their own way. What else did Israel trust in?

answers.text: The multitude of their mighty men

cards.text: So the roar of battle will rise against Israel's people. Friend, this is the part where Hosea's message gets LOUD.

cards.question: Hosea says Israel's fortresses will stand strong through the battle.

cards.text: Hosea compares it to the day Shalman devastated Beth-arbel, when mothers were dashed to pieces along with their children. It's a terrible picture, and Hosea doesn't soften it.
Then Hosea names a place: “Thus it will be done to you, O Bethel, because of your great wickedness.”

cards.question: And when the day dawns, what happens to the king of Israel?

findings.problem: The card says 'Their promises are mere words.' The text says 'They speak mere words' (Hosea 10:4). Calling their words 'promises' renames what the text calls them.

rule.text: Call things what the text calls them.

findings.problem: The question says 'All those broken promises.' The text calls them 'false oaths' used to make covenants (Hosea 10:4). It never says the promises were broken. A false oath is a lie when it's made, which is not the same as breaking a promise later.

rule.text: Call things what the text calls them.

findings.problem: The statement 'Israel has moved far past the sins of Gibeah' can be read two ways. It can mean Israel left those sins behind, which is false. It can also mean Israel's sin has gone far beyond Gibeah's, which a baker could argue is true. Card 1 also says 'they have sinned since the days of Gibeah,' which nearly gives the answer away.

rule.text: No near-matches. A wrong answer never means the same as the right answer, or close to it. If a baker could argue it's right, replace it.

findings.problem: The second half of Hosea 10:9, 'Did not the battle in Gibeah overtake the sons of iniquity?', is never told on any card. It is the verse's own point about what happened at Gibeah, so the baker misses an important detail of the passage.

rule.text: When the baker leaves Prep, they understand the whole passage without missing an important detail.

findings.problem: The joke 'She knows her job and she LOVES it, like me with a fresh batch of dough' is mild and pleasant, not a real laugh.

rule.text: If a line reads like a nice dad being pleasant, push it further.

findings.problem: Shalman shows up for the first time, and the card doesn't say who he is. Scholars don't agree on who he was, and the passage gives no details. Beth-arbel isn't identified either.
findings.question: When the docs require Papa Dorin to say who a new person is, what should he say if that person's identity is uncertain, like Shalman in Hosea 10:14? Should he say nothing, say it's unknown, or leave it to a dictionary pop-up?

findings.problem: Several cards state facts from outside the passage to say who or what something is: 'Judah, the southern kingdom' and 'Jacob, another name for Israel' (stop 2, card 8), 'Samaria, a city of Israel' (stop 1, card 11) and 'Ephraim as another name for Israel' (stop 1, card 14). The docs say outside facts come 'with their reference.' They also say a card cites only its own verses, no wider, and that a choice card cites only the verses of its right answer. None of these outside facts carries a reference.
findings.question: How should an outside fact used to say who someone is get its reference, when a card's verses can only cite what the card tells (or its right answer)? Or are short identifying descriptions like these exempt from needing a reference?

findings.problem: Some cards retell Hosea's predictions in the present tense, as if they are already happening: 'Then the people of Israel call out to the mountains' (stop 1, card 18, where the text says 'Then they will say') and 'Samaria goes with her king, carried off' (stop 1, card 16). Other cards keep the 'will' of the prophecy.
findings.question: In prophetic passages, may Papa Dorin retell predicted events in the storyteller's present tense, or must the cards keep them in the future tense to show they are predictions?
